Ottawa, May 19, 1930.
Famous Players Canadian Corporation, Limited, was incorporated on the 23rd of January, 1920, under the provisions of The Companies Act.

It is difficult to understand why any reference to the government on this subject should be made. The Companies Act does not confer upon the Department of the Secretary of State or any other department of the government any authority to intervene in any action which may be taken by the shareholders in accordance with the provisions of the act. If the provisions of the act have not been completely complied with any relief upon the subject would be afforded by the courts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Rather than unnecessarily take up time in moving the adjournment of the house in order to discuss this matter, I shall simply point out to the Prime Minister that there are three questions which it seems to me might be considered by this parliament and settled by governmental action. The first is in connection with the amendment of the Companies Act so as to provide for the control of a medium, not only of amusement but of education of this type. Considerable discussion has taken place as to whether companies carrying on this business should not be under the control of Canadian directors.
The second question which I have been asked to submit to the house is as to whether or not the present condition is not a violation of the Combines Act, and the third question is as to the rights of minority shareholders.
The question raised by the parties interested must be settled by the courts, as we

Famous Players Corporation
have nothing to do with that. The only-question to be considered is the policy to be pursued in a matter of such national importance, in view of the fact that it is alleged that production, distribution and exhibition of films are controlled by a company controlled and managed in a foreign country. This might create a condition which would necessitate governmental action, and this house should consider whether or not, before prorogation, governmental action should be taken so as to safeguard an interprovincial and a national business. This matter concerns the provinces from British Columbia to Prince Edward Island. It is not only with the films themselves we are concerned, but there is involved in the question the buildings in which such films are exhibited. I suppose the right hon. gentleman has seen the press report of the meeting which took place in Toronto a few days ago, at which meeting a very large number of Canadian shareholders expressed grave concern, not with respect to their investment but with respect to the national aspect of the question. I quite agree with the statement of the Under-Secretary of State that the rights of individual and minority shareholders in matters of this kind do not concern this parliament. That is a matter for the courts, but we should consider the national aspect of the question. The government might well consider the broad question of amendments which might be made to the Companies and other acts to meet the situation.

When the committee were discussing this item on Thursday and Friday of last week, I called attention to the fact that in the province of Quebec a number of factories were deeply interested in the matter under consideration and the bon. member for Lincoln also directed attention to the fact that in his own constituency and elsewhere in the province of Ontario a number of silk factories were also concerned. In order that I may present my views more clearly before the committee, I wish to state generally that this item affects particularly the broad silk industry of this country and importations from Japan of silk of that class and description. The broad silk industry was started in Canada by the incorporation of the Bruck Silk mills at Cowansville, Quebec, in December, 1921. That was the first really substantial effort made with respect to the production of silk cloths in this country. According to returns which are published in the financial journals, that company now has SSOO.OOO invested. It began to market its production in Canada in 1923, and this initial
enterprise was followed by the incorporation in 1923 of two other companies which commenced operations in 1924.
From this small beginning there are to-day eight silk plants in Quebec and six silk plants in Ontario in actual operation, and another plant of very considerable size is projected and I understand is now under way for the production of broad silk alone at Valleyfield, Quebec. The total looms installed number about 1,200, and when the proposed plant at Valleyfield is in operation, 200 looms will be added, making about 1,400 looms in all. In addition to this there are certain Canadian celanese factories, some of them in Quebec, with approximately 500 looms. These factories make a product that is being and has been used in recent months to take the place of Japanese importations. This would make a total productive capacity of about 1,700 looms actually installed, with 200 more about to be installed, or a total of 1.900 looms which will give employment to approximately 1,200 people as wage earners. The proposal under discussion affects all of these people of whom no less than 1,400 are resident in Quebec.
I have gathered from the technical returns published a statement regarding a number of these factories in both Quebec and Ontario. This is an industry which is located largely in towns of comparatively small population where the employment given is of great advantage to the people living in those smaller communities. At Cowansville in Mis-sisquoi county, which is represented by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, there is the Bruck Silk Mills, Limited, which has a capital investment of $800,000. This was the company which was incorporated in 1921 and to which I made reference. According to the latest returns which I could find, it has 240 broad looms suitable for and actually engaged in the manufacture of broad silk cloths. It has 5.600 spindles et cetera. This is a most important industry in Cowansville which, according to recent returns, has a population of less than 1,200.
At Drummondville in the constituency of Drummond-Arthabaska, which is represented by one of my hon. friends opposite, there is a silk company known as Roessel, Louis, and Company, Limited. It manufactures broad silks and has about 1,800 spindles and 100 looms for the manufacture of this special silk cloth.
There is at St. Hyacinthe the Consolidated Silk Mills, Limited. St. Hyacinthe is a manufacturing town of some considerable importance. It has a population, however, under 12,000 people. The Consolidated Silk Mills,

My hon. friend the Minister of Finance was somewhat mistaken, I think the other night with regard to the circumstances under which the present dumping duty against Japan was first levied. I suggested at the time that he was splitting hairs in the discussion, and as he left it to the committee to decide who was splitting hairs I wish to draw particular attention to the law governing the case. Under the customs tariff, chapter 44 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, section 6 was enacted with respect to the special or dumping duty. This clause was enacted so far as I can ascertain in 1907, where it appeared in the statutes of 1907, chapter 11, as section 6. I quote:
In the case of articles exported to Canada of a class or kind made or produced in Canada, if the export or actual selling price to an importer in Canada is less than the fair market value of the same article when sold for home consumption in the usual and ordinary course in the country whence exported to Canada at the time of its exportation to Canada, there shall, in addition to the duties otherwise established, be levied, collected and paid on such article, on its importation into Canada, a special or dumping duty, equal to the difference between the said selling price of the article for export and the said fair market value thereof for home consumption; and such 'special or dumping duty shall be levied, collected and paid on such article, although it is not otherwise dutiable.
Then follow some few lines which do not apply to the present case, and then comes subsection 2, which is all-important. I quote:
6 (2). Excise duties shall be disregarded in estimating the market value of goods for the purposes of special duty when the goods are entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff.
There was there a clear enactment, I suggest, to the effect that a special exemption would be made in favour of exports from those countries which come under the British preferential tariff; but there was a clear and emphatic provision in the statute to the effect that, excepting those exports which come from countries entitled to the British preferential tariff, the foreign excise duties should not be disregarded. Now the amendment proposed by the Minister of Finance to that section which I have just read simply retains the express words of the section as it previously existed and adds the words " or intermediate tariff or any more favourable tariff." So that the clear intention of this amendment is to exempt not only the countries which are entitled to the British preferential tariff, but those other countries which enjoy the intermediate or any more favourable tariff. My hon. friend is proposing now a specific enactment which will have this dual effect. First, it will take from the

In the second place, it gives to the manufacturers of Japan and other foreign countries, which do not come under the British preferential tariff, a much more favourable entry for their exports of silk into the Canadian markets, where they come into competition with the products of our own mills.

When the goods are sold to Canada or any other country outside of Japan that excise tax is not paid. The point I got up to make is this, and it has been made before by the Minister of Finance. Our friends opposite have argued this question from the point of view of protection. This excise tax which involves the application of the dump, and which may serve as additional protection for the Canadian manufacturer, might disappear to-morrow by the action of the Japanese (government, over which we have no control whatever-a circumstance which my hon. friends will admit does not provide a very safe way of protecting any industry, if we want to talk protection. For instance, the Japanese government might put on an excise tax of 50 per cent to-morrow or the next day, or it might wipe out the excise tax altogether. The point I make is this, that it is an entirely fortuitous circumstance which essentially has nothing to do with the matter of tariffs or protection. If my hon. friends argue that because of lower costs in Japan, because labour is cheaper, there should be a higher protection or safeguarding, as my hon. friends might say, of the Canadian silk industry, I should think that is a proper subject of consideration for a higher tariff. But this matter of excise tax is entirely outside our control and should not be regarded as a safe factor in the matter of providing protection, if you wish to call it such, for the Canadian manufacturer. That would be my argument. It does seem to me that it should not enter into the question so far as the dump is concerned. My hon. friends should not forget that the adding of an excise tax to the home price does not preclude our charging customs tax on the value, including the excise tax in the country of origin. It involves only the question of the dump.
Something was suggested about the cost of labour in Japan. I have no doubt that that cost is a great deal lower in Japan than in this country. But I am also told, and I think it is pertinent to the discussion, that whereas there is now the 22i per cent tariff against Japanese silk, the cost of the labour that enters into the manufacture of silk in Canadian mills is only something like 26 per cent. -So the disparity is not as great perhaps as 2419-141
my hon. friends thought. But if it is a matter of providing greater protection, if you like, to the Canadian manufacturer, this does not seem to me the proper method of doing it, because it cannot be depended upon. It may be wiped out at a moment's notice by the Japanese government. I suppose my hon. friend is ready with the words-
Perhaps you will say them for me.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
No. I know what my hon.
friend is thinking of-countervailing duties. These have no application for the simple reason-I am getting away from the subject, Mr. Chairman, because I am getting at what is in my hon. friend's mind-that after all, we have a fixed tariff below which our tariff will not go. Therefore this case is not at all parallel with the other. I have no objection to arguing as to the possible necessity of doing something more for the Canadian manufacturers of silk fabrics, but in that case I think the proper course to take is to raise the tariff, if you like, and that should be done only after the whole matter has been considered by the tariff board.

Is it not a fact that in
1907-I am not certain of the year, but at any rate it was when the Hon. W. S. Fielding was finance minister-this principle was introduced by him and established after a thorough discussion by parliament, that is, as to how the fact of dumping should be ascertained and when the clause should be applied. Why abrogate that principle now without giving some notice? If in the same tariff you had provided for an increase in these tariff items, 560, 560a, 560b and 560c, so as to give a corresponding increase in the regular duty, then there might have been some ground for the argument that the dumpage duty should be wiped out. But my hon. friend is suggesting that we should destroy some six factories in the province of Quebec and seven or eight in the province of Ontario by this change, place their working people on the streets, and then after they are down and out we should come in and ask for increased duties on these particular items. That is a perfectly ridiculous contention it seems to me. Why not allow the principle, which the late Hon. W. S. Fielding, established, with the support of the Liberal party in this house with regard to dumpage, to prevail, until you make some corresponding compensation to these people whose protection you are wiping out to a very considerable extent?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to continue the debate, but I should like to make one observation. I would be very sorry if what my hon. friend appears to fear should happen, that is, the destruction of certain silk factories in this country. But does not my hon. friend know that under a government which, I think, he supported a regulation was passed-not an order in council-exempting these excise taxes from being taken into consideration for the purpose of establishing the dump.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue

No Minister of Customs or
of National Revenue has any power by regulation to avoid the law which is definitely laid down there. That is why it was restored in 1928.

I do not see the force of

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue

My point is that if I find

That would be splitting hairs with greater precision than the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is capable of-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Quite so; but it was illegally withheld from 1918.

I am not going back to
1918 when I was not a member of this house. I do not hold myself responsible for all the peccadilloes of the Liberal party, the Conservative party, the Unionist party or any other party. I say this dumpage is legal under chapter 44, section 6, of the revised statutes of 1927. It has been regarded as legal during

the past two years. It was never enforced against Japan because it was not brought to the notice of the customs department prior to a certain date, which I trust will be fixed by a specific announcement from the minister. But prior to a certain date it was not brought into force against Japan's exports of silk to this country because it was not known here, or if it was known it was overlooked by the customs department, that the 10 per cent consumption tax had been imposed by Japan. Therefore do not ask me to support this proposal because of some illegality which prevailed under an administration years ago. Let us deal with the conditions as they prevail to-day. Up to the first of May legally the tax was in effect in this country. Under that condition our silk factories were able to supply to a large extent the home market, they had gained the upper hand in dealing with Japanese competition. Now you are wiping out 10 per cent of their tariff protection, and you are not giving them any corresponding increase in the regular duties. If the dumpage is to be wiped out, at the same time a corresponding tariff increase should be given. That is my contention.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Is it not true that these silk factories were almost all established at the time when they had not this additional 10 per cent protection on account of the excise tax?

They were established at
that time, but Japan was not sending into this country these classes of fabrics, because the development of their manufacture in Japan is a very recent development, a development whereby Japan is brought into competition with the equally recent development of the silk industry in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend
that it might be necessary to do something: more, but my submission is that what is proposed is not the proper way in which to do it. I think my hon. friend will agree with me if he thinks logically-as he always does-that the proper method, if something should be-done, is by a change in the tariff itself.

I advocated in the house
last Thursday or Friday evening that the more logical way would be to increase the duty on these specific items; but on the other hand we have been dealing with it under the statute which I have quoted, which was passed in 1907 under the Laurier administration, when the late Hon. W. S. Fielding was Minister of Finance. That statute is clear and specific-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
in its terms, and every Canadian manufacturer of silk when he entered upon this new enterprise was aware that the statute then prevailing would in certain exigencies and under certain conditions give him protection in the Canadian market to that extent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
But which might disappear
at any moment at the behest of a foreign nation-something over which we had no control at all.

Quite so. In view of certain provisions in this tariff, my hon. friend should not mention tariffs which come into force at the behest of a foreign nation. It is a provision however which should be considered in dealing with the quantity of protection which should be received by Canadian factories. The fact is that, in this country, we have a tax upon productive energy amounting to nearly 25 per cent of the entire output of the productive activities of Canada, and that tax goes into the municipal, provincial and federal treasuries. We have a business tax upon corporate enterprises, and this tax enters into the cost of commodities. Every tax imposed by this government in the way of direct taxation enters into and increases the cost of production. So that in Japan when they impose a consumption tax it enters no more directly into the real cost or prevailing market price to the consumer in Japan than does the imposition of business, sales and other taxes which are imposed as additional burdens upon our people. Therefore, so long as that statute remains in its present form and so long as the customs tariffs on the articles contained in items 560a, 560b, 560c and 560d remain as they are, I protest against the amendment here suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend knows that so long as the law remains in its present form it will have to be carried out in the same manner as we have been carrying it out since 1928. The Minister of Finance proposes to change the law because he believes that the principle is unsound.
I protest against the change of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Oh, that is your reason.

I assumed that my hon.
friend understood that I was protesting against the change in the law.

We have a peculiar situation before us; we have a minister of the crown changing an excise law, and we have another minister saying it is wrong in principle, but if 2419-14X4
the hon. gentleman wishes to save the manufacturers who are leaning to a certain extent upon that excise law the tariff should be increased.

There is no excise law
affected.

It is strange that certain
things are found to be wrong in principle at a certain time when such principles have been maintained in this house for twenty years. In the words of the Prime Minister, they are vicious principles. The minister adopts the principle and hangs on to it as long as he can, but when it begins to burn his fingers he calls it a wrong principle. The fact that this trade was receiving a certain amount of protection, and in order to cut off that protection it is discovered that the principle is wrong. Then the other minister comes along and states that the tariff should be raised if anything is to be obtained from it. Who has the running of the thing? These people knew nothing about this change, nor did they know how if was going to affect them. They were not invited to attend before the tariff board. How could they ask for a change in the tariff? I suppose the minister found out that no examination into the matter was made by the tariff board. The matter we have in hand is of as much interest to those people as if it were in the tariff. It has been there for the best part of two years. The minister shakes his head, but I would remind him that it was August 15, 1928.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Your colleague stated

I know my colleague
stated that, but it is possible that he has not the facts as clearly as I have them. I ask the minister if he denies that it is two years; of course he will not. They have had the benefit of this tariff and it is now proposed

The other minister, the Minister of Customs, states that he is a protectionist and that the proper way to approach the matter is to go before the tariff board. The result will be that no relief will be given. Improper action is being taken; this matter has not been taken before the tariff board in respect of either the duty, the wages or anything else. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not wish to follow my hon. friend's acrimonious method of discussion-

It may be due to my

speechtext: The hon. gentleman did not mean it that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should again point out to the committee that my hon. friends' statements in regard to the existing law before the amendment are undoubtedly correct. On the other hand, it is also correct that notwithstanding the law in 1919 the government of the day issued a regulation stating that foreign excise taxes were not to be taken into account when arriving at the dump duty.

Was that done by order
in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was done by regulation of the department, authorized by order in council. Prom that day in 1919 until August 1, 1928, foreign excise taxes were not taken into account, in spite of the fact that the law said they should be. This government did not inaugurate that condition; it existed from 1919 to 1928. These silk factories came into existence during the period when the excise tax of foreign countries was not taken into account. My hon. friends will point out immediately that in the case of Japan the excise tax did not come into existence until 1922 or 1923. Still, five years elapsed before any action was taken to consider the foreign excise taxes in levying the dump duty. Then in August, 1928, in some manner it was discovered that the law in this respect was not being complied with; the regulation of 1919

was rescinded and the matter reverted to the condition in which it was prior to May 1, when this budget was brought down.
I am pleased to say that according to my information my hon. friends' apprehensions as to the ruination of the silk industry are entirely unfounded. My hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George and my hon. friend from Lincoln know that the figures which they quoted embrace the whole silk industry, and embrace far more than the portions of it which could possibly be affected by the various excise taxes in Japan being considered with respect to the dumping duty on entering this country.
That is not so with respect to the figures which I gave; they apply to the particular items which I gave in the tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend stated them very cleverly; he used the figures affecting the whole industry. He repeatedly referred to broadcloth looms, whether or not the broadcloth loom end of that mill was an important end of the mill business or a minor end and he included those amongst his figures for the whole industry. I do not blame him-
I gave the number of broad looms as far as I could do so, in order that the minister might see clearly the extent of the industry which would be affected, and which I say is imperiled by this change.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, in his .other figures my hon. friend included many figures which did relate to the whole industry, and which went beyond the broadcloth loom industry.
I defy the hon. gentleman, as a matter of privilege, to mention a single figure of the class he has mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wonder if I could not have the floor, just as a matter of courtesy. My hon. friend spoke for over two hours on this matter.

Do not make erroneous
assertions, then; stick to the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As to the adequacy of the tariff rates actually in effect I am not in a position to say, further than to state that the tariff rates are the same to-day as they have been for a great number of years past; they are exactly the same as they were during that long period from 1919 to 1928, -when this position which we are now trying to rectify did not exist. They are exactly in the same position they were in when the industry was first established; they are 22i per cent under the intermediate tariff and 30 per cent under the general tariff. With respect to the ques-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
tion of how wages affect the matter, my hon. friends have referred to the low wages of Japan and have given some information from the United States in order to show the wages paid in that country. I do not know how authentic that information may be; perhaps we might secure information more directly in regard to that matter rather than just take the evidence of some individual before the United States tariff commission.
However that may be, we have information as to the salaries and wages paid in Canada, and remember this is not wages alone but salaries and wages paid in the silk industry in Canada in 1929. These amounted to $3,820,000, and the total value of the product of the industry is given at $14,476,000, so that salaries and wages all told amounted to approximately 25 per cent of the total products sold. I have not figured it out exactly, but that is approximately correct. That being so I submit that my hon. friends have not a very good case when they represent that this industry is going to be ruined because of the return to-day to the exact position in relation to that tariff which they occupied up to August 1, 1928, as stated by my hon. friend from Lincoln, or March, 1929, as stated by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George. For the moment I do not care which date is correct, but I say that it is too much to ask us to believe that this industry is going to be ruined by being returned to the condition under which it was established and under which it operated during all the years from 1919 to 1928. It is too much to ask us to believe that it is going to be ruined, especially when its payroll, salaries and wages, amount to about 25 per cent or 26 per cent of the total value of the commodity. These people know perfectly well that if they think their tariff is not high enough and if they can demonstrate that fact publicly, they can apply for a reference to the tariff board, and I would be delighted to give them that reference. However, in my view that is no justification for maintaining a condition which is manifestly unsound in principle.
My hon. friends discussed this question as though silk were the only commodity which would be affected. As a matter of fact this matter affects the whole of Canada's tariff relationships with the world. No other country of which I have knowledge has a provision whereby a dumping duty is created because an exporting country has an excise tax upon a particular commodity. That condition does not exist anywhere else. My hon. friends confined their discussion entirely to silk, but we do not know what day an excise regulation in some other country may bring about a similar
condition with respect to other commodities. Frankly, if I thought this change would have the effect of ruining the industry and throwing people out of work I would not propose it for a moment, but I have become so accustomed to hon. gentlemen opposite making that statement with respect to anything proposed that I require a little more evidence than their mere say-so before I am prepared to believe that ruin will result.
Evidently the minister intends to have a trial and see how far it can go in that direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, that is not fair
either.

I desire to say a few words under this item, because there is involved in this discussion a principle of far-reaching effect upon the working people and the industries of Canada, particularly the working people. British Columbia is the third province in the Dominion in the value of manufactured products, and Vancouver ranks fourth among the cities. In 1927 the gross value of our manufactured products was $246,000,000, and to-day it could be properly estimated at about $2SO,000,000 or $290,000,000. In 1927 there were 47,740 employees with a payroll of $56,000.000; to-day on the basis of the statistics furnished by the Dominion government, probably there would be about 60,000. In 1927 there were 1,509 plants with a capital investment of $325,000,000'.
A few days ago we had presented to parliament and passed a measure known as the Fair Wages and Eight Hour Day Act, 1930, the principles of which I heartily support. The words of one section of that bill are significant as embodying the need in this country for some protection to labour and the industry of Canada from the unfair competition of the oriental countries such as China and Japan. The section to which I refer is in these words and has reference to contracts with the government of Canada:
All persons in the employ of the contractor, subcontractor, or of any other person doing or contracting to do the whole or any part of the work contemplated by the contract shall be paid such wages as are generally accepted as current from time to time for competent workmen in the district in which the work is being performed for the character or class of work in which they are respectively engaged; provided that wages shall in all cases be such as are fair and reasonable	
The point I wish to make in that regard, Mr. Chairman, is one which very vitally concerns the people of British Columbia and particularly the workers in the industrial life of that province. My hon. friend from Lincoln

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
produced an authoritative statement of comparative wages in connection with the silk manufacturing business in Canada, the United States and other countries; the statement shows that for the forty-eight hour week, male weavers in the silk industry in the United States received $34.27. In Canada they receive $29; in Japan they receive a wage of $2.54, which with food allowance, amounts to about $4 and in China male skilled workers receive $1.80 per week. What I desire to bring to the attention of the government is this: We in Canada, and particularly those interested in these matters in British Columbia, realize the need of a reasonable protective tariff which will protect not only industries but the labour that goes into our industrial life from the competition of those workers in the orient who receive such low wages. It is utterly useless to put low tariffs upon goods coming into this country; to make regulations and laws respecting fair wages and the eight hour day and at the same time allow products to come in from Japan and China where weekly wages of $4 and $1.80 respectively are paid as compared with $29 in Canada for the same class of work. I desire to place that principle before the house and bring it to the attention of the Minister of Finance. Reductions have been made in a great number of these items, which will unnecessarily and adversely affect the working people and industrial life of this country. My submission is that when the government entered the waters of protection, instead of putting one foot in they should have gone in and had a swim for the good economic health of Canada. Had they done that a great number of industries in Canada would have been beneficially affected and the working population of this country would have been much better off. However, that was not done and we in the west are faced with competition from countries where labour is so cheap and where the standards of living are not comparable with those obtaining in this country. The arguments presented by my hon. friends should receive the favourable commendation of the minister and consideration should be extended to the adverse effects and possibilities of competition from oriental countries. No policy is sound or statesmanlike which is not founded in the welfare and happiness of the masses of our people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. I am very chary

My hon. friend may have heard of him. He was not a prohibitionist, but a great temperance advocate. He was a member of the British house and he was fond of asking questions designed to elicit information which would be of service to him advancing the cause he had at heart. On one occasion during the Ashanti war he asked a question as to the proportion of casualties among total abstainers in the Ashanti expeditionary force and he was staggered1 when he got the information that 50 per cent were killed and 50 .per cent died. That looked terrible, but being a persistent old gentleman he made further inquiry and found that there were only two total abstainers in the Ashanti expeditionary force, one of them having been killed and one having died. That illustrates that the percentage method of approach does not always reveal the facts of the situation. The bean growers to my mind made out a case for their request before the tariff board; hence I am proposing now to grant it.

Leaving the percentage
alone, I say it is four times as much. If that will not suit the Minister of Finance, I do not know what will. I know of no other country that has increased its tariff four times as much as before. I would move:

speechtext:

Mr. DUNNING': Y*

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It will be observed that of the beans that came into Canada last year the greater part came from treaty countries, Japan and Belgium chiefly, our imports from those two countries approximating 170,000 bushels, as against 110,000 bushels from the United States and the small quantity of 18,000 bushels from the British Empire. I take it, therefore, that it is perfectly clear that the imposition of the tariff at the present rate is to encourage the production of beans at home and to protect Canadian agriculture. That is what it must be for; it could not be for British trade. The minister will observe that the rate for treaty countries is now 90 cents per bushel, and that last year the duty was 22i cents with respect to the two treaty countries principally affected. Do I understand it to be the minister's view that an increase of 400 per cent protection is exactly what is required to develop the bean industry in Canada? I do not want there to be any misapprehension about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The protection is not 400 per cent. My hon. friend knows better than that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The increase in the tariff is from 22j cents a bushel to 90 cents a bushel for treaty countries, from which last year we bought the major part of our bean requirements. That is the intermediate tariff. That is an increase in the tariff of 400 per cent. Do I understand it to be the government's position that it was necessary to increase the bean duty 400 per cent to supply adequate protection to the Canadian bean grower?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not going to talk
in percentages.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But this is a clear case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In my judgment the
bean growers made out a case with respect to the production of beans in Canada, and with respect to oriental competition particularly, and continental competition, but not to the same degree. Beans can be grown in Canada. It is a commodity which we should be producing in many different parts of this country. That is the position.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think the minister is
perfectly frank. This increased duty is imposed for the benefit of the Canadian farmer and the producer of beans in Canada. What the percentage increase is, of course, is a 2419-142.J
matter of no great moment to my friend from Weyburn as long as the protection is adequate and sufficient. So far as we are concerned, we desire to see the bean industry fostered and safeguarded and benefited. We are not assuming any responsibility as to the extent to which the hon. gentleman may think it desirable to impose taxation for that purpose, but how my hon. friend from Lisgar would have made the welkin ring in days gone by at 400 per cent increase in the tariff.
It is not 400 per cent, but 300 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Four times 22| is 90.

The increase is 300 per
cent.

speechtext:
Well then, 300 per cent.
I am glad that the hon. member for North Battleford is satisfied that 300 per cent of an increase in the tariff is reasonable and adequate protection, but he objects to 400 per cent as a little too much. How the welkin has rung in days gone by at an increase of 10 or 20 per cent! How any increase at all has been denounced by some hon. gentlemen! How the cry has gone forth that the farmer never could benefit from protection! Where is the consumers' league now? Page Mr. Deachman.
It never should benefit the farmer, did the hon. gentleman say?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Never could; I am quoting the hon. gentleman and the consumer's league.
Never could ultimately.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Now we have it; I suppose we have reached the ultimate. I think if my hon. friend will study Archbishop Trench's book on words he will find that the ultimate has now been reached. How my hon. friend from Weyburn used to denounce the Conservative party as the party of high protection! BROWN: I beg my hon. friend's pardon. For . my part I never have used those percentages, I recognize what folly it is to talk in percentages only, as I pointed out the other day.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am so glad the hon.
gentleman never used those figures. Of course, he never could have used them, because the Conservatives never made such increases. Look at the happiness with which they accept this three hundred per cent increase! What a happy crew!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

I should say so. Any

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: They make a mess of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They often do, they make a great mess of it-as the hon. minister will discover shortly when he gets up to Waterloo. Let us have no misunderstanding. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) moves in amendment that item 47 be free under the British preference and be the same as it was previously, namely, 22J cents per bushel under the intermediate tariff, and 25 cents per bushel under the general tariff.
I find at page 164 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms the following quotation from the 13th edition of May, page 544. dealing with standing order No. 60:
Proposals for the variation or modification of taxation can therefore be made in the committee; but these proposals must be grafted 
upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, and must not affect the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year. Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, of equivalent amount,-[DOT]
The amendment in my opinion conflicts with that authority in two particulars:	First, it
would affect the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year; secondly, it is not an equivalent amount. Therefore I rule the amendment out of order.

On the point of order,
may I refer you, Mr. Chairman, to paragraph 556 at page 165 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, where it is distinctly stated :
The house can make amendments which diminish the amount of reduction of taxation, or postpone the day when the reduction takes place, although the amendments may increase to that extent the charges proposed to be levied upon the people.
So long as an existing tax is not increased, any modification of the proposed reduction may be introduced in the committee-
I am introducing it in the committee; I am not increasing the tax at all, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am afraid the hon.
gentleman does not appreciate the fact that the house may do certain things that the committee may not do. We are in committee of ways and means at the present time.

May I repeat my citation again:
So long as an existing tax is not increased, any modification of the proposed reduction may be introduced in the committee on the bill,-
Do you rule, Mr. Chairman, that a member of the committee cannot move to reduce a tax?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, that is my ruling.

Then I think you had
better revise it, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is it not rather a question, Mr. Chairman, as to the stage of the proceedings at which action of this kind may be taken? I am not familiar with the rule, but as I understand it action may be taken at a certain stage in the proceedings.
I have repeatedly heard the Minister of Finance reduce or increase taxation in committee of ways and means.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A minister of the crown may move to reduce or increase taxation, but not a private member.

Mr. Chairman, I think you will find that that is wrong. A minister of the crown can move to increase, but any member can move to decrease taxation.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
It has been done in this house many times.

Mr. Chairman, will you explain what is meant in paragraph 556 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms where the author cites May as authority for the statement:
The house can make amendments which diminish the amount of reduction of taxation,-
Does it mean that only a minister of the crown can make such an amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I understand, Mr. Chairman

I am not arguing for or against the point of order-the house is competent to reduce taxation, but it is a question as to the stage of the proceedings at which such action is in order. The section that my hon. friend quoted refers, I believe, to the stage of a bill. We have not yet reached that stage; there is no bill before the house; this is a committee of ways and means. By and by what this committee does takes the form of a bill; that bill then goes to the committee of the -whole, and there I believe it is competent for a private member to move such an amendment as that now moved by my hon. friend from East Calgary. I am not clear whether or not it is competent for a private member to do it at this stage. You, Mr. Chairman, will have to decide that.

Read it.

I will read it. This will be found at page 165 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms:
The house can make amendments which diminish the amount of reduction of taxation, or postpone the day when the reduction takes place, although the amendments may increase to that extent the charges proposed to be levied upon the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will notice the expression "the house"; not, "the committee of ways and means."

Allow me to complete t'he citation:
So long as an existing tax is not increased, any modification of the proposed reduction may be introduced in the committee on the bill, and is regarded as a question, not for increasing the charge upon the people but for determining to what extent such charge shall be reduced.
We have not reached the bill yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The citation explains the position as I stated it a few moments ago. Any proposed reduction may be introduced in the committee on the bill.
I may move my amendment in committee on the bill?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes. Shall the item
carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. I notice that some 10,000 bushels of beans came from the United Kingdom and paid duty under the general tariff. The total of British importation amounted to 18,000 bushels. The general tariff at that time was 25 cents a bushel; it is now $1.20 instead of 25 cents a bushel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
So that my leader was not very far astray when he referred to the increase in percentage. The increase is made from 25 cents a bushel to $1.20 a bushel, or almost 400 per cent.
It is 480 per cent.

It is almost a 400 per cent increase. So that there is an increase of 300 per cent on the intermediate tariff and 400 per cent on the general tariff. I am a pretty good protectionist, and I could not ask for better than that. I may tell my hon. friends that I will not oppose it.
iMr. MANION: I would like to ask the minister why in this case only he changed the measure from bushels to pounds. The bushel measurement is applied to buckwheat and barley; cornmeal is measured by the barrel and oats by the bushel. The original rating last year was per bushel, but it is changed this year without notice to a poundage basis. There is no note to show that the old rate was figured by the bushel. speechtext: No.

It is rather peculiar that the other commodities are measured in terms of bushels or barrels, whereas in this case, where there is such an immense increase over the rate applicable last year, there is a change. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Some of the public may be more easily deceived.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I would not say that. As a matter of fact, there are two reasons. This might be a convenient place, after the attention the minister has given to the bean growers, to give us some reason for the government discarding its past policy and accepting the present one. How many beans came from Great Britain under the British preference during the year ending March 31, 1929?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There were 18,000 bushels from Great Britain, of which I believe 8,000 bushels were entitled to preference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not the information before me in the form necessary to supply an exact answer for my hon. friend. The hon. member for Lincoln confirms my statement that 10,000 bushels came in under the general tariff.

What is going to haippen to the plank in the Liberal platform which calls for free trade in foodstuffs?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are going to put it along with a number of planks in my hon. friend's platform.

May I ask the Minister of Finance why it is that in one year he has changed his mind? I have a vivid recollection of his saying one year ago, in reference to beans: Increase the duty on beans for 300 growers?-Nothing doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman cannot quote that; bis contention is not correct, and he knows it.
I think the minister gave me an incorrect answer to my question. Only 547 bushels came in under the British preferential tariff; that is my interpretation of the information at my disposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not look at the figures. My hon. friend from Lincoln was bind enough to supply them, and I accepted them.
I would like to have the figures cited correctly. I say that there were only 547 bushels.
I have before me the 1929 returns, and they show that under the treaty 7,714 bushels came in from the United Kingdom.
That is correct.
Valued at $26,277.

That statement also is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I have stated on
numerous occasions, any industry in Canada, whether it be the bean growers, the piano manufacturers, or any other, can appear publicly before the Tariff Advisory Board. Application can be made for either an upward or a downward revision in the tariff, and I am prepared to examine the facts brought out at that public hearing. I ask hon. members to examine those facts, and if they do not think the facts brought out justify the result now before the house, let them vote upon it.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
Would the minister accept the recommendations or findings of such a board? Can the public feel that if they go to the expense of presenting a case, the minister will accept the recommendation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No government of Canada will ever delegate its primary responsibility, or place it in the hands of an appointed board; the decision must rest with the government, which must exercise its judgment upon the facts. In this case, rightly or wrongly, we have exercised our judgment in respect to the information received and_ the facts brought out at the public hearings, which are of public record.

Are the tariff adjustments contained in these proposals the findings of the tariff board, or are they instances in which the government, exercising the reservations which have just been referred to, has made alterations differing from the findings of the tariff board? In other words, do the budget proposals express the findings of the tariff board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The tariff board is part
of the Department of Finance. The officers of the tariff board are officials of the Department of Finance, and the procedure is not and never has been by way of recommendation. The procedure is and always has been a consultation between the minister and his officers with respect to the facts brought out at the public hearings.

I think the remarks of
the minister justify a little more questioning on our part. To my mind this brings out a very essential fact which overshadows all others. It is this: If either party in this house appeals to the country on a definite policy, are the people entitled or are they not entitled to consider that party seriously? Are these policies to be discarded on their return to office, simply through political expediency? That is the main issue on this budget, whether the government can discard with impunity its professions of the past. That is the question the people of this country are asking to-day.

Then the
minister thinks that this measure will be of material advantage to the bean growers? Has he come to that conclusion on the advice of the tariff board? Is that Why this change has been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A number of years ago
the government announced as its policy the setting up of a tariff advisory board to hear public representations on tariff matters,
whether those representations were for upward or downward revision. As a low tariff man I cannot take the ground that all changes in the tariff must be downward, if I have accepted the provision that there shall be an inquiry and if I have taken the position that I am prepared to consider the facts whatever those facts may be. That is the position which this government has taken and which it takes to-day.
So far as the future fortunes of the bean growers are concerned, they are like all other agriculturists. My hon. friend will remember the raisin pool in California. I had occasion to examine it on three different occasions in the hope that it would give some information as to the proper course to follow in respect to other products of the soil. I found this, which has been true with respect to other commodities: The pool definitely raised the price of raisins in California; there is no doubt about that. The effect of raising the price of raisins, in the course of a few years, was to increase materially the acreage of land in California devoted to growing raisins, and when more people got to growing raisins there were more raisins and as a consequence the prices did not remain up. That is an actual fact; we know it to be true. If an industry dependent on the cultivation of the soil is prosperous, more people go into that industry.
Is that not true of industry generally?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It*is not so much true
of other industries as it is of the agricultural industry.

When did you become
a convert?

It suits the minister to
talk from the standpoint of the agricultural industry. That applies just as much to any other industry as it does to agriculture. That is the protectionist argument.

I take it, then from the remarks of the minister, that perhaps this measure may work a temporary benefit, but in the long run he is of the conviction that, as happened with the raisin pool, it will work to the detriment of the producer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not prepared to
say that.
Am I to infer that from the remarks of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not prepared to say that definitely. Somebody over here said that I was a recent convert to this idea. I may

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
tell him that away back in 1924 at the British Empire Cooperative Conference, when the cooperative consumer societies of Great Britain were urging that the course we were following in Canada as grain growers would have the effect of raising the price of bread in England, my answer was that it is easy to increase the production of breadstuffs; the extension of wheat acreage in a year, given profitable wheat raising, will ensure the production of a sufficient quantity to take it out of our power as growers to force the prices up to unreasonable levels. I have been preaching this doctrine for years with respect to agriculture.
I was not referring to that as far as the minister was concerned; I was referring to his recent conversion to protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, I am not a protectionist.

I should like to ask the
Minister of Finance if he can tell us exactly to what we are restricted at this stage of the discussion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from East Lambton is getting up again, but before he does so I should like him to answer one question. I understand that beans aire grown to some extent in his part of Ontario. Has he any bean growers in his own riding?
Yes, I have.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Many?
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister if the tariff on this item has been raised on the representations of the bean growers themselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

In view of the remarks
of the minister with respect to an hon. member to my left, in which he implied that the hon. member had very few if any bean growers in his riding, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance if he has been converted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In a recent speech in this house the

Minister of Trade and Commerce used almost exactly the same arguments as those which have been proffered by the Minister of Finance. In that connection I should like to ask the minister how many furniture builders he has in his own constituency?

The minister said something about the facts being brought out by the tariff board, and I think he also stated that this revision is in the interests of the bean growers. Would he mind telling me what outstanding fact it was that led him to concludue that the increase would be in the interests of the bean growers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I listen with some care
to representations of farmers in connection with their own industry, and in my judgment the case of the bean growers was well prepared and well presented. I would listen to wheat growers just as well; I have done so many times and expect to do so again.

May I just ask the minister one question before he leaves the subject? In view of the fact that the minister has changed his mind in regard to the need of protection, or the amount of protection under this item, is there any reason, just supposing by some accident he got into this same position next year, why he might not change back again?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can tell my hon. friend that in the light of the facts put before the tariff board I am content with this decision. I am not going to pretend that five or ten years hence further facts may not be developed at a hearing before the tariff board on the same subject by the same people, which might even convince me that conditions have changed, but I see no immediate likelihood of that happening.

Why not say four years
hence? There will be another election then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I had no reference to
that.

There was in the old

Wheat flour and semolina when imported from a country which imposes a customs duty on wheat flour or semolina, manufactured in Canada, per barrel: 30 cents; 50 cents; 50 cents.
That was the tariff brought into effect, by the way, on June 6, 1919. That was a countervailing tariff.

That is a fixed duty.

speechtext:
To my mind it is a
restricted countervailing tariff, for the reason that if another country does not impose a duty on a like article coming from Canada, this item does not apply.
They cannot raise our duty. It is not a countervailing duty.

speechtext: It is so regarded. Under the old item we imposed a duty of only fifty cents no matter how high the other country's duty went. Under the countervailing proposals now before the committee on various items, our tariff is fixed at what we consider proper, but in addition to that our tariff goes up or down as the case may be.

Is the minister not quoting

That is not countervailing;
it is a fixed tariff.

tariff.

speechtext:
I am not sure if it is
with respect to wheat.

speechtext:
Section 11 reads:
If the President of the United States, under authority of the United States Tariff Act of 1922, determines to reduce the duties imposed by such act on the following articles, that is to say:-cattle; wheat; wheat flour; oats; barley; potatoes; onions; turnips; hay; fish as enumerated in paragraphs-
And then it gives the paragraphs.
-the governor in council may by order in council make such reductions of duties on such articles imported into Canada from the United States as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for such reductions on Canadian products imported into the United States.

in the tariff that while our rate of duty on wheat with respect to the United States remains at twelve cents, there shall be a countervailing provision upward and we have in addition the provision to enable us to meet them in any reductions.

speechtext: What I do not understand about the matter is this. We have factories in this country making macaroni. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:

There have existed in our tariff, for years-

They may find that to-day the Canadian producers are somewhat averse to this particular tariff

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And the coon came down.
I am not worrying about the coon. I am not talking about that just now. Mr. Savage is, I understand, a well known merchant and I am sure he is well known to the leader of the opposition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He is one of my supporters.

This is from Mr. Savage:
Consumer:
Have you given any thought to the proposed tariff changes brought down in the budget by
Mr. C-hapIin.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What is my hon. friend
quoting from?

A casual examination reveals startling information. All cars of fruits and vegetables clearing customs since May 1 at all ports in Canada, the duties in my opinion will be more than double that previously charged. The importance of some of these duty charges I submit the following:-
The government in their tariff proposal is I10! ^untcut increasing duty on the commodity itself, but are charging a duty on packages-
That is directly contrary to the statement made a minute or two ago.
-and where a specific duty is levied, which is in 90 per cent of the cases, in addition to the weight of the commodity the weight of the package is included in the weight for duty. Even ice that is inside of containers to assure the safe arrival of perishable goods, is assessed.
Then he gives a number of instances of the duty that will be paid. I do not know that I need trouble the committee with them, but they are very large.
Put them on Hansard.

He continues:
As an example, in the instance of cabbage the duty will be equivalent to $25 per ton.
Onions, $15 per ton.
Carrots in bulk, $20 per ton.
Cauliflower will be approximately, $50 per ton.
Rhubarb, $25 per ton.

Potatoes, $10 per ton.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
Bear in mind all the above is the minimum duty. There can be a higher duty assessed, namely taking advantage of the ad valorem tariff, or whichever is the higher, you pay your money and the government take their
choice.	,	, ,,
1 wish to point out that 75 per cent of the fruit and vegetable business-
In this connection what the minister proposes will meet it.
-that is competitive with the United States that the season in which they are received covers the producing season in Canada of from thirty to ninety days. In the instance of tomatoes these are imported the year around into Canada and produced in Canada for a period of not more than three months, hothouse production excepted. Therefore the consumer is paying the same tariff the year around to protect the grower for a commodity that lie can only supply for from thirty to ninety days.
The proposed increase will undoubtedly mean increases in the price of the Canadian produced article as well as the imported article, and this will reflect in higher cost of living to our people of Canada, which will reflect itself iu the necessity for higher wages, which will not permit our manufacturers and producers to be able to compete with other countries, especially so when we are producing to supply world markets, which is a substantial policy of the Canadian government at the present time.
He goes on further to say this, and I think this is a very striking part of his letter:
The government and growers of Canada before allowing the present proposal to pass, should study the question in relation to the commercial condition in all of Canada. Surely it is not the intention of the government to adopt a policy that will tend to injure industry and agriculture itself. The Canadian consumer is and has been a very tolerant people, patriotic in fact, but in my opinion when they find a certain industry receiving a monopoly and trying to force an intelligent people to pay according to their views I feel certain they will be in a losing fight if the tariff as presented in the budget is passed. The people of Canada will undoubtedly tell the government when they go to the polls, that they are not believers in giving protection to the extent of what can be called a monopoly. I feel sure however, that inasmuch as our whole fiscal policy for the last sixty years has been built around a moderate tariff, that the consumer is still inclined to see a fair and reasonable duty levied for the purpose of revenue. I wish here to point out that the great producing areas of Canada are amply protected on all imports of fruit and vegetables when you consider the extra freight rates that have to be paid on like commodities as those produced in Canada. In the instance of importing to this market from British Columbia there is a rate on apples of seventy-one cents which is undoubtedly an excessive freight charge; a freight rate of forty-two cents on vegetables as against California of $2.10 per hundredweight and on vegetables from $1.65 to $1.85. In addition the icing charges are double and sometimes treble on all cars of fruit and vegetables as compared with British Columbia. Ill the case of Washington and Oregon the rates are a little lower than from California. It
therefore does seem to me that the position of our western Canadian grower in particular is a most favourable one as compared with the growers across the line from Canada who have to compete against the production of fruit and vegetables that come into their territory from all parts of the United States duty free. I therefore challenge the growers of Canada to prove through any bench of judges or an independent commission, that their position is worse than border states of the United States.
It just simply cannot be proved.
The Canadian producers that are clamouring and hollering for these prohibitive duties should concern themselves in production, producing more to the acre and varieties and qualities of fruit and vegetables that are demanded by our Canadian markets.
Then the writer says:
An excellent way of killing a home market is to raise prices. It is much more readily slain in that way than by prohibiting foreign imports. Moderate prices should lead to increased consumption. The fruit growers should be extremely grateful to the opposition developing to their demands. If they have their own way it is quite possible they will kill then-own market by driving the people to the use of foreign fruits which compete indirectly with their own production. You cannot force up the price of apples, pears, peaches, grapes, plums, and cherries, without leading to an increased demand for oranges, bananas, and pineapples, always providing of course that the price of tropical fruits is not increased by the artificial restriction of tariffs. The present position of the fruit grower in Canada is far from doleful, despite tales of woe from the weeping rooms raised for the purpose of drawing sympathy from the thoughtless and uninformed citizens. I know of no other instance where by protection a people are guaranteed a profit. Success can only' come when they learn to rely on their own resources instead of asking government pap and make the already overtaxed consumer pay for it.

Mr.. BENNETT: It has.
Mr.. GLEN: Of course it has. The main argument I have addressed on this question bears out the contention in Mr. Savage's letter that any tariff imposed on these articles must certainly be paid by the consumer by way of increased price. We have had the exemplification of that since the introduction of the budget. We know that the price to the consumer is greater, and those of us who live in the west know that he is not in a position to pay it. I think that these schedules ought not to be in this budget at all. It is the fault of our budget system that there may be a great many things in the budget with which you can agree and some things to which you are strongly opposed, but you have to vote either for or against the budget as a whole. You will find things that you know are detrimental not only to Canada but particularly to the people you represent. That is the case with this budget, more perhaps than with any other. The protective principle on agricultural products has been introduced, against which I must strongly protest and which I repudiate. I have never stood for it and I do not intend to stand for it. These fruit and vegetable schedules are detrimental to the best interests of Canada, arud they should be reconsidered. We cannot move amendments, but in view of the expressions of opinion coming from western Canada, where we shall suffer more than people in any other part of this country because of our long hauls, I strongly urge the Minister of Finance to reconsider these fruit and vegetable schedules in their entirety and come back with some method of alleviation.

Has the hon. gentleman
courage to move an amendment himself?

It is not a question of
courage. If you want to move an amendment, move it yourself.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is very strange, after this wholesale condemnation of the fruit and vegetable schedules by the hon. member for Marquette to find among the names of those who voted for the budget the name of Glen (Marquette). Surely the voice I have just heard is still the voice of that same gentleman, and the observations to which we have just listened were made by the same hon. gentleman who voted for the budget the other evening. Why this protestation now and the vote the other evening? Why support the government when it fears for its life, and oppose it when opposition is of no consequence? What is the reason?
Politics.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon. friend from
Southeast Grey says "politics," and she usually is light. The hon. gentleman cannot be ignorant of the fact that during the last twenty-four months from one end of this country to the other, alike upon the prairies, in British Columbia, in Ontario and in eastern Canada, I have pointed out that all that was required for the purpose of enabling the Canadian fruit and vegetable grower to have an equal opportunity with his competitors was that at particular seasons of the year tariffs be made available that would prevent the dumping of foreign surplus products upon the Canadian market, thus destroying the home market of our own producers. Surely the hon. gentleman must recall that. Certainly in the Okanagan country, in as strong terms as possible, I referred to it. Then, lest it might be said that these observations were made where fruit and vegetables were grown, and not for the benefit of the consumer, I made the same observations in the cities of Edmonton and Calgary. I made the same observations in Winnipeg and Saskatoon and in eastern Canada. Why? Because in 1922, after a close analysis of the situation, it was realized by all parties in the house, except my friends to the extreme left, that it was desirable that the Canadian fruit and vegetable grower should have a chance to sell his product at a decent price as against competition that came to him by reason of the surplus products from other markets being pressed upon the Canadian market at a particular time of the year. Last year, for instance, just as our fruits were maturing in British Columbia, I happened to beatYahk junction, where seven carloads of American fruit had come in destined for the prairies. They represented the tail end of the American crop. The supplies necessary to meet the demand of the American people in Oregon and Washington had been provided, and the surplus was being sent forward at a price that enabled them to undersell the British Columbia producer. Some of these producers-there were gentlemen on the other side of the house, one at least, who passed through there a short time afterwards-actually showed me the results of their operations which spelt for them financial ruin, complete. They have been endeavouring to build up an industry in that particular area. I said to our friends on the prairies: Which do you prefer? To destroy industry in its entirety in the Okanagan and in British Columbia, or to enable it to live? Do you want in this country a foreign monopoly of

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
fruit whereby any price desired could be charged by the foreigner? That was the question. I never saw any difficulty at any time upon the part of fair-minded Canadian consumers in opposing such a possibility.
What about the monopoly in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I cannot answer that
question; for I am not sufficiently familiar with the situation to answer it. But this I will say, that in the section which I visited last year there was no evidence of a monopoly.

Was there not
a committee controlling the price?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Not in southern British
Columbia where I was. They showed me exactly what they were doing, the competition they had to meet, and the efforts they were making to meet it. They did explain to me that they had a cooperative marketing board.
And a committee of direction, which would haul any man to court who dared sell under their directions as to price.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
They have a statute in

The committee
controls the price of our supplies on the prairies.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am not at all familiar
with its operations in that sense beyond what the hon. member now tells me. The statute to which I referred is a provincial statute-
The committee are asking that American fruit be shut out except subject to their dictation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I trust that my hon. friend may be able to induce his Minister of Finance to see the error of his way, rather than seek to get one who sits on the opposition side of the house to reform his methods. The hon. gentleman will remember that in 1922 we passed a statute whereby the minister was empowered to make recommendations as to the valuations upon which prices were based for duty purposes at given seasons of the year. That is, it did not limit the time within which it might be invoked. It has already been explained to the house that that statute was put in operation during the all
too short life of the administration of Mr. Meighen, and it was found that its operation afforded the relief sought without increasing the price to the consumer. That is the main thing-without increasing the price to the consumer. The result was that it gave the Canadian market to the Canadian producer at a given time of the year.
Does the hon. gentleman say that that order in council did not increase the price to the consumer?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Certainly.
Never?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
No. What was more, it was clearly indicated in Winnipeg, Calgary and elsewhere that the prices of the commodities referred to in the order in council had not been increased thereby over the fair market prices that prevailed even in other countries. That was the effect of it. Now what has happened? This government has placed upon the statute book a tariff on fruit and vegetables which applies all the year round. It is divided into two parts, an ad valorem tariff and a specific tariff, and whichever is the higher prevails. Its application in the city of Winnipeg and in Calgary is pointed out in the letter which my hon. friend from Marquette has just read. It was also pointed out in the Winnipeg Tribune, in the Winnipeg Free Press, and in other western papers. They were dealing not with theories but with actual oarloads of fruit and vegetables that came in from the United States at a time when they did not compete with the Canadian-grown fruits and vegetables; for we were not marketing them then, so that they did not in any sense interfere with the operations of the Canadian producer. I took the trouble since the budget was introduced to look a.t one of the markets in the city of Toronto, to see exactly where the vegetables that were being sold on that market came from. I observed that some of them came from Texas, some from the far Pacific slope, some from other parts of the United States. Now, at this season of the year, we are not growing cabbages, we are not growing strawberries, and we are not growing other fruits and vegetables that come in from the United States. So there is no reason why the consumer should have to pay an enhanced price by reason of the fact. The tariff that was in force before the government messed it up, as they did the other day, gave adequate protection to the producer at a time when he did not desire to interfere with his fellow-Canadians getting imported fresh vegetables and fruits that he was not growing. The act

as it stood in actual operation provided a solution that was satisfactory to the people. My hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) put upon the order paper a resolution demanding that the order in council should be rescinded. In due course his notice of motion disappeared and the order in council was rescinded. Then there was a great gathering downstairs in the railway committee room. I do not propose to go into the details of that gathering-they were so admirably dealt with by my friend from Yale (Mr. Stirling) the other evening-beyond saying that in the discussion it became apparent that the vegetable and fruit producers themselves were satisfied with the operation of the order in council under the statute passed in 1922.
Well, they might be.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will my friend object to that? Now this government came in. Look at what they have done. At a time when protection is not required the maximum duty is applied; at a time when the maximum duty is required the minimum is applied. Instead of improving the position of our vegetable and fruit producers-as in the case of beans-they make it worse. Mark this, the government must follow some line of policy. They have made an increase of 400 per cent in the case of beans. Why do they not follow this policy in regard to fruits and vegetables? They have not done what the producers asked for before the tariff board. On the contrary they have adopted a principle of their own, which principle, as I have indicated is the application of a specific or an ad valorem tariff, whichever is the higher, with the result that the higher tariff will prevail at a time when it is not necessary, and the lower at a time when the higher tariff is required; and it is all the year round. What happened? The government of the day-shall I say?-compelled its supporters from the prairies to support that proposal.
Nothing of the kind.

speechtext: Oh, how amusing, Mr. Chairman, is the sophistry of the hon. gentleman from Saskatoon! He says: "I voted for committee of ways and means and we are now in it." That is his answer. That is the budget for him. That is the national policy now: "I voted for commitee of ways and means and we are now in it." Go and tell the citizens of the prairies that. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

There is the story of the hon. gentleman. Why, he looks his part.
